title: Nearly Instance Optimal Sparse Matrix Approximation from Matrix-Vector Products
classifications: Theory of computation → Design and analysis of algorithms
abstract:
A large body of work studies the problem of learning an approximation to an implicit matrix 𝐀 ∈ ℝ^{m×n} that is only accessible implicitly via matrix-vector product queries (matvec queries) of the form 𝐱 → 𝐀𝐱 or 𝐱 → 𝐀^T𝐱. Of particular interest are methods that learn a near-optimal approximation with a fixed sparsity pattern. For example, we might want to learn a near-optimal diagonal, banded, or arrow-head approximation to an implicit matrix 𝐀. 
Naturally, the number of matvec queries required to solve this problem depends on the sparsity pattern, which can be encoded as a binary matrix 𝐒 ∈ {0,1}^{m× n}. The query complexity of previous algorithms scales with quantities like the total number of ones in 𝐒, its maximum column/row sparsity, or the chromatic number of its "conflict graph". These quantities are incomparable: for a given 𝐒, parameterizing by one might yield lower query complexity than another.
In this work, we unify and tighten these prior results by providing a nearly sharp characterization of the matvec query complexity of sparse matrix approximation. Generalizing a definition from graph algorithms, let the degeneracy, degen(𝐒), denote the smallest number k so that, if we iteratively delete all rows and columns of 𝐒 with ≤ k ones, we are left with an empty matrix. We show that a near-optimal approximation to 𝐀 with sparsity pattern 𝐒 can be learned with Õ(degen(𝐒)) matrix-vector product queries, and Ω(degen(𝐒)) queries are necessary, for any sparsity pattern 𝐒. Moreover, unlike prior work based on graph coloring, all of our methods run in polynomial time.

          Abstract
A large body of work studies the problem of learning an approximation to an implicit matrix
A ∈ Rm×n that is only accessible implicitly via matrix-vector product queries (matvec queries)
of the form x → Ax or x → AT x. Of particular interest are methods that learn a near-optimal
approximation with a fixed sparsity pattern. For example, we might want to learn a near-optimal
diagonal, banded, or arrow-head approximation to an implicit matrix A.
    Naturally, the number of matvec queries required to solve this problem depends on the sparsity
pattern, which can be encoded as a binary matrix S ∈ {0, 1}m×n . The query complexity of previous
algorithms scales with quantities like the total number of ones in S, its maximum column/row
sparsity, or the chromatic number of its “conflict graph”. These quantities are incomparable: for a
given S, parameterizing by one might yield lower query complexity than another.
    In this work, we unify and tighten these prior results by providing a nearly sharp characterization
of the matvec query complexity of sparse matrix approximation. Generalizing a definition from graph
algorithms, let the degeneracy, degen(S), denote the smallest number k so that, if we iteratively
delete all rows and columns of S with ≤ k ones, we are left with an empty matrix. We show
that a near-optimal approximation to A with sparsity pattern S can be learned with Õ(degen(S))
matrix-vector product queries, and Ω(degen(S)) queries are necessary, for any sparsity pattern S.
Moreover, unlike prior work based on graph coloring, all of our methods run in polynomial time.

    1      Introduction
Matrix approximation based on matrix-vector products has emerged as a fundamental
primitive in numerical linear algebra and optimization [1, 3, 4, 13, 16, 30, 31, 32, 34, 35,
37, 38, 39, 47, 50]. Recently, the problem has also found applications in scientific machine
learning (SciML) as a powerful yet tractable special case of operator learning [8, 9, 10, 22, 51].
    In the basic setup, we are given access to black-box matrix vector products (abbreviated
“matvecs”) with A and AT for some unknown matrix A ∈ Rm×n . I.e., we can evaluate
Ax1 , AT y1 , . . . , Axq , AT yq for adaptively chosen vectors x1 , . . . , xq ∈ Rn and y1 , . . . , yq ∈
Rm . “Adaptively” means that the choice of xi , yi can depend on all previous queries and
their results. Given the results of all queries, the goal is to find a near-optimal approximation
to A from some pre-specified family F ⊂ Rm×n . I.e., find B̃ ∈ F satisfying1 :
        ∥A − B̃∥F ≤ (1 + ϵ) · min ∥A − B∥F .                                                               (1)

           Natural examples for the approximation family, F, include low-rank matrices, hierarchi-
       cally structured matrices, butterfly matrices, and more [37, 39, 30]. As one example result,
       when F is the class of rank-k matrices, (1) can be achieved with O(k/ϵ1/3 ) matvecs [4].
           In applications, we are interested in algorithms based on matvec queries because it is
       often far more efficient to compute matvecs than to produce A explicitly. Common settings
       include when A is the Hessian matrix of a high-dimensional optimization problem, with which
       matvecs can be computed efficiently via autodiff [48], or when A is an integral transform
       that can be applied efficiently using the Fourier transform or Fast Multipole Method [34].
       Another example arises when A is the inverse of a matrix B. While producing A requires
       matrix inversion, and thus O(n3 ) time, matvecs can often be computed by solving a linear
       system involving B, which takes time O(n2 ) or less when A is well-conditioned [6],

       1.1      Sparse Matrix Approximation
       An important special case of the matrix approximation problem is when F contains all
       matrices with some fixed sparsity pattern.2 One example is the class of diagonal matrices [6,
       5, 24]. Diagonal matrices are widely used to approximate Hessian matrices in optimization [7,
       21, 42, 57] or inverse matrices in statistical applications [28, 54]. Other fixed-sparsity families
       of interest include block-diagonal matrices, banded matrices, and matrices whose non-zeroes
       correspond to a known graph (e.g., a low-dimensional mesh) [18, 30, 54, 55].
           Any such family can be encoded by a binary matrix S ∈ {0, 1}m×n representing the
       sparsity pattern, where a one at position (i, j) in S indicates that entry (i, j) is allowed to be
       non-zero for B ∈ F. The optimal Frobenius norm approximation to A with sparsity pattern
       S is easy to write down: it is S ◦ A, where ◦ denotes the entrywise product. However, it is
       not typically possible to compute S ◦ A using a small number of matrix-vector products. In
       particular, while we can read any single column or row of A using one matrix-vector product
       (with a standard basis vector), S’s ones could be distributed among many columns/rows.
           As such, prior work has focused on approximation algorithms. For the special case of
       diagonal approximation, it is known that the popular Hutchinson’s estimator finds a near-
       optimal diagonal B̃ satisfying (1) with O(1/ϵ) matvec queries, and no algorithm achieving
       the same approximation guarantee can use asymptotically fewer queries [6, 24]. Optimal
       query complexities are also known, e.g., for banded and block diagonal matrices [2].
           For more complex sparse families, however, the optimal query complexity is often unknown.
       A number of prior results provide generic results that give query complexities depending
       on certain properties of S. For example, if S has at most s ones in any row (or column)
       then [2] shows that a (1 + ϵ) error approximation can be learned using O(s/ϵ) products with
       random p  Gaussian vectors. It can also be shown that, if S has at most nnz(S) total ones,
       then O( nnz(S)/ϵ) matvecs suffice, no matter how the ones are distributed [1, 20].
           Another line of work studies algorithms based on graph coloring [17, 18, 19, 29, 41, 49, 54].
       Such methods are typically only analyzed in the easier recovery setting, where A itself is
       assumed to be sparse. I.e., S ◦ A = A, and thus the optimal solution to (1) has 0 error. In
       this setting, the complexity of these methods depends on the chromatic number (or related
       properties) of various graphs related to S. For example, [19] observes that, if we can partition
       the columns of S into k subsets, each consisting of columns with disjoint support, then

any matrix with sparsity pattern S can be recovered with k matvecs. The smallest such k
corresponds to the chromatic number of a “conflict” graph, G, associated with S: G has a
vertex for each column and an edge between any two columns with overlapping support.
    Finding an optimal coloring of G (to come up with a suitable set of query vectors) is NP-
hard, so heuristic approximation methods are typically used instead. NP-hard optimization
problems also arise in the implementation of more complex coloring-based algorithms with
refined query complexities, which have been studied in work by Mccormick [41], Power and
Toint [49], Coleman and Cai [17], and others.

1.2      Our Contributions
Our paper simplifies and generalizes this prior work by identifying a single combinatorial
parameter of the sparsity pattern, S, that, up to logarithmic factors, completely characterizes
the matvec complexity of learning a near-optimal approximation with sparsity pattern S.
Specifically, generalizing a notion from graph theory, we define:

▶ Definition 1 (Degeneracy of a Sparsity Pattern). Consider a matrix S ∈ {0, 1}n×m . For
a positive integer k, delete all columns and rows of S with ≤ k ones, and then repeat this
process on the smaller matrix that remains until no further columns or rows can be deleted.
If we are left with an empty matrix, then we say S is k-degenerate. The degeneracy of S,
denoted by degen(S), is the smallest value of k such that S is k-degenerate.

If S was the symmetric adjacency matrix of an undirected graph, G, then degen(S) would
exactly correspond to the degeneracy of G, which is also known as the k-core number,
width, or graph linkage [33, 36].3 Our main algorithmic result is that degen(S) bounds the
complexity of approximating an unknown matrix A with sparsity pattern S:

▶ Theorem 2 (Upper Bound). Let S ∈ {0, 1}n×m be a known sparsity

          We complement Theorem 2 with a nearly matching lower bound for any sparsity pattern
       that holds even for adaptive methods (Theorem 2 uses non-adaptive queries4 ):

       ▶ Theorem 3 (Lower Bound). For any sparsity pattern S ∈ {0, 1}m×n , δ < 1 and any finite
       C, no algorithm which queries less than degen(S) matvecs with A or AT can return, with
       probability 1 − δ, a matrix B̃ satisfying ∥A − B̃∥F ≤ C · minB:B=S◦B ∥A − B∥F .

       The proof of Theorem 3 is simple, following from the fact that any sparsity pattern S with
       degeneracy degen(S) must contain a submatrix with at least degen(S) ones in every row
       and column. It can be shown that, in the recovery setting where A = S ◦ A, recoverying
       even this submatrix in A requires ≥ degen(S) matrix-vector product queries. In the recovery
       setting, minB:B=S◦B ∥A − B∥F = 0, so a lower bound for recovery implies a lower bound for
       approximation for any finite C. This proof is detailed further in Section 3.
       ▶ Remark 4. As mentioned, in the recovery setting, we can learn any A with sparsity
       pattern S with exactly 2 · degen(S) matvecs (see Lemma 10). Theorem 3 thus implies that
       our recovery algorithm is essentially “instance optimal”: no method can improve on its
       complexity by more than a factor of 2 for any sparsity pattern. At the same time, it avoids
       the computational intractability of, e.g., solving a graph coloring problem.
       ▶ Remark 5. For the approximation setting, there is a gap of O (log(m + n)/ϵ) between the
       upper and lower bounds of Theorem 2 and Theorem 3. We believe the log(m + n) term
       can possibly be eliminated from the upper bound. However, the O(1/ϵ) term is inherent.
       There are sparsity patterns for which Ω(degen(S)/ϵ) matvecs are necessary to learn a (1 + ϵ)-
       approximation. E.g., see [2] for a lower bound of Ω(s/ϵ) for s-banded matrices. On the other
       hand, there are sparsity patterns where O(degen(S)) matvecs suffice. A simple example
       is when S has only a single non-zero column, i. Such a pattern had degeneracy 1 and an
       exactly optimal approximation with the sparsity pattern (i.e., with ϵ = 0) can be learned
       with one matvec: simply read A’s ith column by multiplying with a standard basis vector.

2.2    Problem Formulation
We study algorithms that can only access an unknown target matrix A ∈ Rn×m through left
and right matrix-vector products (i.e., “matvec queries”). We formalize this model as follows:

       ▶ Definition 6 (Matrix-Vector Product Query Model). An algorithm in this model can issue
       queries of the form (x, s), where x is a vector and s ∈ {L, R}. If s = R, the algorithm receives
       query response Ax for a fixed, unknown matrix A ∈ Rn×m . Otherwise, if s = L, the algorithm
       receives AT x. A q-query algorithm is one that issues q queries, (x1 , s1 ), . . . , (xq , sq ), where
       the choice of (xi , si ) can depend on the outcome of all previous i − 1 queries.

       In the numerical analysis literature, methods implemented in the matvec query model are
       often referred to as “matrix-free” or “implicit” methods. In this work we consider solving
       two closely related problems in the matrix-vector product query model:

       ▶ Problem 7 (Sparse Matrix Recovery). Given a sparsity pattern S ∈ {0, 1}n×m and query
       access to a matrix A where A ◦ S = A (i.e., A has sparsity pattern S), recover A.

       ▶ Problem 8 (Sparse Matrix Approximation). Given a sparsity pattern S ∈ {0, 1}n×m and
       query access to an arbitrary matrix A, find B̃ such that B̃ ◦ S = B̃ that satisfies:

            ∥A − B̃∥F ≤ (1 + ϵ)     min     ∥A − B∥F .
                                  B:B◦S=B

       Note that we always have minB:B◦S=B ∥A − B∥F = ∥A − A ◦ S∥F .

       Observe that Problem 8 is strictly harder than Problem 7: if we have an algorithm that solves
       Problem 8 for any finite ϵ, then when run on any matrix A with sparsity pattern S, it must
       return A exactly to achieve multiplicative (1 + ϵ) error (since minB:B◦S=B ∥A − B∥F = 0).
            When evaluating algorithms for these problems in the matvec query model, we are
       primarily interested in minimizing matvec query complexity. This is motivated by the fact
       that, in many applications, computing Ax or AT x is a computational bottleneck, so query
       complexity closely correlates with computational cost. Indeed, there has been significant
       recent interest in proving tight upper and lower bounds on the matvec query complexity
       of natural linear algebraic problems like trace estimation, linear system solving, eigenvalue
       computation, and more [11, 12, 14, 15, 23, 43, 44, 46, 52, 53, 56].
            That said, other facets of an algorithm implemented in the matvec query model are also
       of interest. For example, ideally we should be able to efficiently compute the query vectors,
       x1 , . . . , xq , and we should also be able to efficiently construct B̃ from the obtained responses.
       All of the algorithms in this paper run in time polynomial in the matrix dimensions n and m.
            There is also interest in algorithm that require limited “adaptivity”, meaning that the
       queries can be chosen all at once (“non-adaptively”) or in a small number of rounds. Low
       adaptivity algorithms allow for increase parallelization query computation, which can lead to
       speedups in practice. All algorithms considered in this paper are fully non-adaptive.

        3      Lower and Upper Bound for Sparse Matrix Recovery
       We begin by observing that, for any sparsity pattern S, degen(S) lower bounds the matvec
       complexity of recovering a matrix A with sparsity pattern S. As discussed in Section 1.2,
       our main lower bound in Theorem 3 follows as an immediate corollary.

       ▶ Lemma 9. For any sparsity pattern S ∈ {0, 1}n×m , no algorithm can solve Problem 7 with
       any positive success probability using < degen(S) matvec queries.

       Proof. We first observe that, S must contain a submatrix with at least degen(S) ones in every
       row and column. This is because, if all submatrices had a row or column with ≤ degen(S)
       ones, then by definition, the matrix must have degeneracy < degen(S).

                    ′   ′
    Let S̄ ∈ {0, 1}m ×n denote this submatrix, where m′ ≤ m and n′ ≤ n, and let ℓ′ =
max(m′ , n′ ). S̄ contains at least ℓ′ · degen(S) ones. Now, consider the easier problem of
recoverying a matrix A that is only non-zero on the non-zero entries of S̄. Every multiplication
by A on the right by a vector x yields a vector with at most m′ non-zero entries, each of
with is a linear combination of a subset of entries in A (those contained in a single row).
Likewise, every multiplication by A on the left by a vector x yields a vector with at most n′
non-zero entries, each of which is a linear combination of a subset of entries in A.
   Accordingly, no matter how our query vectors are chosen, if we issue q matvec queries, we
obtain at most q ·ℓ′ linear equations in the unknown entries of A. It is impossible to determine
these entries unless q · ℓ′ ≥ nnz(A) ≥ ℓ′ · degen(S) (since we have an underdetermined linear
system [30]). In other words, we must have q ≥ degen(S) to determine A.                        ◀

    With Lemma 9 in place, it is natural to ask how close we can get to the limit of degen(S)
matvec queries for solving Problem 7. Surprisingly, we show that a simple, non-adaptive,
polynomial time algorithm solves the problem with 2·degen(S) matvec queries. This is despite
substantial work on more complex coloring-based algorithms for Problem 7, which require
solving NP-hard optimization problems to select query vectors, as discussed in Section 1.1.

       computing additional matrix-vector products. We simply update R by subtracting off ÂZ,
       which yields R = (A − Â)Z. Similarly, we update L = AT W by subtracting off ÂT W to
       yield L = (A − Â)T W. From these matvecs, we proceed to learn all rows and columns in
       A − Â with ≤ d unknowns. We repeat the process until S is all zeros and Â = A.
           The correctness of the algorithm rests on the fact that all subsets of ≤ d rows from Z and
       W that we consider have full row rank. This holds simply because there are only a finite
       number of such subsets, and each has full row-rank almost surely [25]. The runtime of the
       algorithm is also clearly polynomial in n and m.                                             ◀


           4    Near-Optimal Sparse Matrix Approximation
       We conclude by providing an Õ(degen(S)/ϵ) query algorithm for the harder problem of finding
       a near-optimal sparse approximation to an arbitrary matrix A, which proves Theorem 2.
       The basic approach is similar to the recovery algorithm from Section 3. Using standard tools
       from randomized numerical linear algebra (specifically, Lemma 12), it is not hard to show
       that multiplying A on the left and right by O(degen(S)/ϵ) random Gaussian vectors suffices
       to near-optimally approximate any row and column with ≤ degen(S) non-zeros.
           Once we have done so, a natural approach would be to subtract off our approximation
       to A and iterate on the residual. However, this leads to dependency issues: unlike the
       recovery setting, where we almost surely learn the exact values of rows and columns, in
       the approximation setting, our residual is a random matrix that depends on our random
       Gaussian queries. This prevents a direct argument along the lines of Lemma 10, since the
       same Gaussian queries cannot easily be “reused” on the residual matrix.
           We deal with this dependency by simply drawing a fresh set of random Gaussian vectors
       at every iteration of the algorithm. Naively, this could be a disastrous idea: it is possible to
       design sparsity patterns where the number of iterations scales with the matrix dimension.
       For example, let S be the adjacency matrix of a path graph on n nodes. This pattern has
       degeneracy 1, and if we iteratively peel off rows/columns with 1 non-zero, it will take n/2
       iterations. Our sample complexity will thus scale with n, instead of the desired O(1/ϵ).
           The fix is simple: it is not hard to prove that, if we peel off rows and columns with
       sparsity ≤ 4 · degen(S) instead of ≤ degen(S), then we can bound the number of iterations
       by O(log n + m). The only cost is a small increase in the number of Gaussian random vectors
       required per iteration (which scales with the sparsity of the rows and columns learned).

       on the remaining matrix. After log2 (m + n) rounds we are left with an empty matrix.

 5      Conclusion and Future Directions
Our work nearly resolves the complexity of fixed-sparsity pattern matrix approximation (and
recovery) in the matvec query model, showing that the degeneracy of the sparsity pattern
characterizes query complexity. Some questions remain open, however. For example, can we
remove the log(m + n) factor in Theorem 2 so that it matches the lower bound in Theorem 3?
Additionally, is it possible to implement Algorithm 2 using only “unstructured” query vectors
(e.g., random Gaussians) instead of the “masked” random vectors we currently use?
    It is also interesting to ask if our generic results for sparse families can be extended to
other classes of matrix families. For example, sparse families are a special case of linearly
parameterized matrix families. A linearly parameterized family consists of all matrices that
                       Pq
can be written as i=1 ci Bi for a chosen set of coefficients c1 , . . . , cq ∈ R and fixed basis
matrices B1 , . . . , Bq ∈ Rm×n [30]. It is know that, in the recovery setting, such matrices
                               √
can always be learned with q matvecs [1]. However, many linear families (including sparse
families) require fewer, often on the order of q/n. Is there a simple parameter of {B1 , . . . , Bq }
that governs the query complexity? What about general, non-linear matrix families?
